blocks.en: Hello, young explorers, and welcome back to Michael's Morning Listening!
Today we have two surprises for you: a boy who borrowed more books than any other young reader in his state, and a bear that looks white but is not white at all.
Ready?
Let's go!
In Malaysia, there is a boy named Alif.
He is thirteen years old, and he loves books more than anything.
His little public library is just a short walk from his house, and Alif calls it his second home.
Reading has built a strong bond between Alif and his little library.
After school, Alif takes a short rest, and then he reads.
At night, after his homework is done, he reads again.
Book by book, the numbers accumulated: in one year, Alif borrowed 1,378 books from the library!
That is more than three books every day.
Soon the library's statistics told an amazing story: no other young reader in the whole state had borrowed so many books.
The librarians approved a special prize for him, and they named him the top young borrower of the year.
Alif reads real paper books, not screens.
He says it is easier to understand a paper book, and easier to share what he learns with others.
When he grows up, he wants to be a science teacher.
Meanwhile, his love of reading is already teaching everyone around him one simple lesson: a small library card can open a big world.
Now, from a warm library in Malaysia, let's travel far north, to the frozen Arctic.
There lives the polar bear, the great white bear of the ice.
But here is a secret: the polar bear is not white at all!
Look closely at one hair of its coat.
It is not white.
It is transparent, like a tiny glass tube, and it is hollow inside.
The hair has no white color in it at all.
So why does the bear look white?
Because sunlight bounces around inside all those tiny clear tubes, and the light that comes back to our eyes looks white.
It is a trick of the light!
Under all that clear hair, the bear's skin is black.
Black skin is good at soaking up the sun's warmth.
And under the skin there is a thick layer of fat.
Together, the clear coat, the black skin, and the fat work like a warm winter jacket: even in freezing wind, very little warmth leaks out.
The white look is also perfect camouflage.
On the ice, a white bear is almost invisible, so seals do not see it coming.
But the bear's real colors are a surprise: clear hair, black skin, and a clever design that keeps it alive in one of the coldest places on Earth.
Here's today's idiom: 'walking on air.' When you are walking on air, you are so happy that you feel like you are floating!
Here's an example: 'When Alif heard he was the top young borrower, he was walking on air all the way home!' Have you ever felt like you were walking on air?
Let's think about our stories: a boy who read 1,378 books, and a bear that looks white but is not.
First: if you could borrow any three books from the library today, which three would you pick?
Second: the polar bear's coat is a trick of the light — what other animal tricks can you think of?
Talk about it with your family!
That's all for today, young explorers.
Keep reading, keep wondering, and may you always feel like you are walking on air!
See you tomorrow!
